description: Five visitor-accessible rounds across Northern Ireland: the Open Championship's Dunluce Links at Royal Portrush, the legendary dunes of Royal County Down, Portstewart's championship Strand Course, the cliff-top classic at Ardglass, and tournament parkland at Galgorm Castle.
intro: Northern Ireland packs two of the world's most celebrated links into an island smaller than some U.S. states — and nearly all of its headline golf is open to visitors. Everything on this list is bookable without a membership, from Open Championship venues to a cliff-top links with a medieval castle for a clubhouse. Most visitors base in Portrush or Newcastle and work outward; plan at least five days if you want all five, and book the big names months ahead.

sections.heading: 1. Royal Portrush — Dunluce Links, Portrush
paragraphs: The Dunluce Links at Royal Portrush is the course that brought The Open Championship back to Northern Ireland — host in 1951, 2019 (won by Shane Lowry), and again in 2025, the only venue outside England and Scotland to stage the championship. Founded in 1888 and largely shaped by Harry Colt's 1929 redesign, Dunluce is links golf in its purest form: towering dunes, the North Atlantic on one side, and one of the most intimidating one-shotters in golf — the par-3 Calamity Corner, where a deep ravine guards the green. A second 18, the Valley Links, sits alongside it.

Visiting Dunluce requires a genuine handicap: men need 18 or better and women 24 or better, with proof and (for many visitors) a letter from their home club. Visitors are welcome on weekdays except Wednesday and on weekend afternoons, and tee times book up months ahead, so start with the club's online booking as soon as your trip dates are set. Pair it with the Valley Links for a 36-hole day, and note the course is walking-only — caddies are available and worth it when the coastal wind gets up.

sections.heading: 2. Royal County Down — Championship Links, Newcastle
paragraphs: Few courses in world golf are spoken of in more reverent tones than Royal County Down. Founded in 1889 and extended to 18 holes by Old Tom Morris (with later work from James Braid, Harry Colt, and Donald Steel), the Championship Links weaves through enormous dunes inside the Murlough Nature Reserve, framed by the Mountains of Mourne on one side and Dundrum Bay on the other. The famous bearded bunkers — deep sand traps with overhanging lips of marram grass — and a collection of deliberate blind shots make it one of the great examination papers in golf. The par-3 4th and the blind, plunging par-4 9th are among the most photographed holes anywhere.

Visitor play on the Championship Links is limited to Mondays, Tuesdays, and Fridays (mornings and afternoons), Thursday mornings, and Sunday afternoons, and tee times are in heavy demand — book through the Secretary's Office as early as the club allows, ideally the better part of a year out. A handicap is required, and because of the blind shots a caddie or fore-caddie is strongly recommended on a first visit; visitors often have one arranged. Budget-friendly travelers should note the shorter 18-hole Annesley Links, also on site, as an easier second round the same day.

sections.heading: 3. Portstewart — Strand Course, Portstewart
paragraphs: Portstewart is the insider's pick on the Causeway Coast: a 54-hole club (three 18-hole links) founded in 1894, whose championship Strand Course is widely regarded as one of the finest in Ireland. The front nine is the show — massive dunes, elevated tees, and an opening hole called Tubber Patrick that drops some 425 yards from a high tee into the dunes, often called the best starting hole in golf. The current Strand routing dates to Des Giffin's 1980s redesign, refined with help from European Golf Design. Two more courses, the Riverside (par 68, along the River Bann) and the historic Old Course (par 64), make 36-hole days easy.

Visitors are welcome on the Strand on weekdays and on Saturday afternoons, with a handicap required; booking in advance is essential. Portstewart sits minutes from Royal Portrush, so pair the two on consecutive days or combine the Strand with a relaxed second round on the Riverside. The back nine is flatter and more forgiving than the dunes-heavy front, so don't judge your whole day by the scorecard on the 9th.

sections.heading: 4. Ardglass Golf Club — Ardglass, County Down
paragraphs: Ardglass is the round you'll tell people about. Founded in 1896 in a fishing village south of Belfast, this cliff-top links hugs the Irish Sea so tightly that the water is in view from every tee and every green, and comes directly into play on eight holes. The clubhouse sits in Ardglass Castle, parts of which date to around 1405 — reputedly the oldest clubhouse in golf. The modern routing is largely the work of David Jones, with holes like the par-3 2nd (Howd's Hole), a 167-yard shot over a rocky inlet, and a knee-trembling par-5 11th where the sea guards the entire right side.

This is an easy add-on to a Royal County Down day: Ardglass is about 30 minutes from Newcastle and under an hour from Belfast. Visitors are welcome and can book online with instant confirmation — far less friction than the two headliners. Play here on a travel day or as a relaxed second round; the wind off the Irish Sea demands creativity rather than brute force, and the small firm greens reward the bump-and-run.

sections.heading: 5. Galgorm Castle — Ballymena, County Antrim
paragraphs: After four links, Galgorm Castle offers something different: the only parkland course in Northern Ireland to host the Irish Open (2020, on the DP World Tour), plus the history-making 2019 ISPS Handa World Invitational — the first tri-sanctioned event across the DP World Tour, LPGA, and Ladies European Tour. Designed by Simon Gidman and opened in 1997 within a 220-acre estate, the Castle Course is a water-in-play parkland bounded by the rivers Maine and Braid, with an oxbow lake setting the scene at the par-4 4th and 15th. The 17th-century Jacobean castle is visible from the 10th green.

Galgorm is the easy logistics play on a Northern Ireland trip: it's roughly equidistant from Belfast, Derry, and the Antrim coast, and visitors are welcome on weekdays and weekends with advance booking. The Galgorm resort next door — thermal spa, golf academy with Toptracer, and family-friendly restaurants — makes it a natural base or a rest-day round for non-golfing travel companions. Expect excellent conditioning and fast greens, and club selection matters more than firepower on the riverside holes.
